435.title: The three young men (Daniel 3)
435.hook: in the furnace they sing all ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord, a song the Church prays on Sundays
435.carry: all ye works, bless the lord
435.howItsDone: The canticle of the three young men from Daniel 3 is prayed at Morning Prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours on Sundays and feasts, and it is a traditional prayer of thanksgiving for priests after Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two wisdom books and one faithful friend. Your line was a friend is treasure. Did you tell yours? Day four hundred thirty-five, and a new week.

King Nabuchodonosor of Babylon sets up a golden statue, sixty cubits high, on a plain. The order goes out: when you hear the music, the trumpet, the flute, the harp and all the rest, fall down and worship the statue, or be thrown into a burning furnace. The band strikes up, and the whole empire goes down on its face. Except three young Jews in the king's service: Ananias, Azarias and Misael, given the Babylonian names Sidrach, Misach and Abdenago. They stay standing. The king, furious, gives them one more chance and asks: what god could deliver you out of my hand?
screen: `A GOLDEN STATUE, AND A BAND.` → `THREE YOUNG MEN STAY STANDING.` → `WHAT GOD COULD DELIVER YOU?`

segments.voice: Their answer doesn't bargain. Our God is able to save us from the furnace. But if he will not, know this, O king: we will not worship your gods. Not because they're sure of rescue. Even if not. The king has the furnace heated seven times hotter, so hot that the men who throw them in are killed by the flames. And the three walk around in the middle of the fire. Here Catholic Bibles hold a passage that some Bibles don't. In the Greek text of Daniel, which the Catholic Church receives as scripture, a long passage comes at this point: a prayer of Azarias in the fire, and then a song. Bibles that follow the Hebrew and Aramaic text, as Protestant Bibles do, leave it out or print it separately among the Apocrypha. The angel of the Lord comes down into the furnace, the text says, and drives the flame out, and makes the middle of it like a cool, wet wind. And the three begin to sing. In Latin it's the Benedicite, from its first word: bless. In the Douay-Rheims: "All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him above all for ever." Then the song calls on everything by name. Angels. Sun and moon. Stars. Showers and dew. Fire and heat. Cold and frost. Nights and days. Light and darkness. Mountains, seas, whales, birds, beasts. And from inside a furnace, they tell fire and heat to bless the Lord. The Church still prays this canticle at Morning Prayer on Sundays and feasts, every creature called in turn.
screen: `BUT IF HE WILL NOT.` · `SEVEN TIMES HOTTER.` · `A SONG IN THE GREEK DANIEL.` · `FIRE AND HEAT, BLESS THE LORD.` · then, large: `ALL YE WORKS OF THE LORD, BLESS THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless one thing by name. Settle, and breathe. Look around you, or out the window, and let your eyes land on one thing that is simply there. The light. A tree. Rain. The cup in your hand. Your own breathing. Name it. The song does exactly this: it names a thing and calls it to praise God just by being what it is. If you pray, you can borrow the song's own pattern with one of its lines: sun and moon, bless the Lord; nights and days, bless the Lord. If you don't, just let yourself be glad that this one thing exists. The bell holds the time.
Benedicite. Latin for bless, the first word of the song of the three young men in the furnace, calling every creature to bless the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: all ye works, bless the lord. Today, name three things you see on your way and let each one remind you of the song. Day four hundred thirty-five.

436.title: The seven books (the deuterocanon)
436.hook: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1–2 Maccabees are in Catholic Bibles; many Protestants call them the Apocrypha
436.howItsDone: Catholics hear readings from the deuterocanonical books at Mass, at weddings (Tobit), funerals (Wisdom) and in the prayers for the dead (2 Maccabees), the same as any other book of scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three young men sang in the furnace and called every creature to praise. Your line was all ye works, bless the lord. What did you name? That song, by the way, is part of today's story. Day four hundred thirty-six.

Try this sometime. Put a Catholic Bible and a Protestant Bible side by side and count the books. The Catholic one has seventy-three: forty-six in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New, as the Catechism counts them. The Protestant one will usually have sixty-six; the Westminster Confession, a Protestant statement of faith, lists them by name. The New Testaments match exactly. The difference is all in the Old Testament. Seven books, plus extra passages in Esther and Daniel, like the song from the furnace we heard yesterday. Same faith in Christ, same Gospels, and a different-sized shelf. So what are those seven, and how did that happen?
screen: `SEVENTY-THREE OR SIXTY-SIX.` → `THE NEW TESTAMENTS MATCH.` → `SEVEN BOOKS, AND SOME PASSAGES.`

segments.voice: The seven are Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and First and Second Maccabees. Catholics call them deuterocanonical. Canon comes from the Greek kanon, a straight rod used for measuring, and so a rule, and so the list of books measured as scripture. Deutero means second. And the second doesn't mean second-rate. It means their place in the list was settled later, after some discussion. Catholics hold them to be inspired scripture, fully. Here's the history, as plainly as possible. Before Jesus, Jews in the Greek-speaking world used a Greek translation of their scriptures, the Septuagint, and its collections included these books. The early Church, mostly Greek-speaking, read that Bible. North African councils around the year 400 list them as scripture. Saint Jerome, translating from the Hebrew, had doubts and set them in a separate category, though he translated some of them anyway. In his German Bible, Martin Luther gathered them into a separate section between the Testaments, calling them Apocrypha: books not held equal to scripture, but useful and good to read. The Council of Trent in 1546 answered by defining the Catholic canon with all seven included. The first King James Bible printed them too, between the Testaments, and later printings could leave them out. Today the Jewish Bible doesn't include them. The Orthodox churches include them and a few more. Protestant confessions like Westminster don't count them as scripture; the Church of England's Articles say they are read for example of life, but not to establish doctrine. And in a Catholic Bible they sit right in among the others. Over the next week we'll open four of them.
screen: `KANON: A MEASURING ROD.` · `SECOND, NOT SECOND-RATE.` · `SEPTUAGINT, JEROME, LUTHER, TRENT.` · `WHO READS THEM, AND HOW.` · then, large: `THE BOOKS BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find Tobit in a Catholic Bible. If you have one nearby, open it to the table of contents now. In a Catholic Bible, Tobit comes after Nehemiah, which the Douay calls Second Esdras, and Judith follows it. Find it, open to the first page, and read only the first verse. If you don't have one, picture the shelf instead: forty-six books, and seven you may never have opened. Settle, and breathe. Then ask yourself which part of the Bible you've never actually read. If you pray, you can ask for a little curiosity. The bell holds the time.
Deuterocanonical. The seven Old Testament books, and parts of Esther and Daniel, whose place in the canon was settled later; Catholics receive them as scripture. Today's word.
Your line: the books between. Today, read one page of Tobit, or just its first few verses, before tomorrow's lesson. Day four hundred thirty-six.

437.title: Tobit's journey (Tobit 1–6)
437.hook: a blind father, a son on a journey, a dog, and a stranger who turns out to be the angel Raphael
437.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Raphael with Michael and Gabriel on September 29 and ask his prayers for travelers, the sick, and those seeking a spouse; the Book of Tobit is read at weekday Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven deuterocanonical books, and how they came to sit in Catholic Bibles. Your line was the books between. Did you find Tobit? Today we open it. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

Tobit is an old man in exile in Nineveh, an Israelite far from home, and he has a dangerous habit. When his people are killed and their bodies thrown out unburied, he goes out at night and buries them, even after the king's men come looking for him. One evening, worn out from burying, he lies down by a wall and falls asleep, and droppings from a nest above fall into his open eyes. He goes blind. He's poor now, quarrels with his wife Anna, and prays to die. And on the very same day, far away in Media, a young woman named Sara is praying the same prayer.
screen: `AN OLD MAN WHO BURIES THE DEAD.` → `BLINDED UNDER A NEST.` → `TWO PRAYERS ON THE SAME DAY.`

segments.voice: The book tells us both prayers were heard at once, and that God sent the angel Raphael to help them both. The characters don't know that. We do. Tobit remembers he once left money in trust with a kinsman, Gabelus, in a city in Media, far to the east. So he sends his son Tobias to fetch it. Tobias doesn't know the road, so he goes out to find a guide, and there's a young man standing there, ready, as if he'd been waiting. He says his name is Azarias, a relative, and he knows the way. He's Raphael. Nobody in the story finds out until the very end. So the two set off, and the story adds a lovely detail: the dog went with them. One of the only good dogs in the whole Bible, trotting along behind an angel and a boy. On the first night they reach the river Tigris, and Tobias goes down to wash his feet, and a huge fish leaps out at him. He cries out. The guide says: take hold of it, and drag it to land. Keep its heart, its gall and its liver; they'll be needed for medicine. Raphael is a Hebrew name, and it means God heals. That's the shape of the whole book: a blind father, a grieving young woman, a son sent out on an errand, and healing walking beside them unrecognized. Catholics keep Raphael as a patron of travelers and of the sick, with his feast on the twenty-ninth of September, alongside Michael and Gabriel.
screen: `A SON SENT EAST FOR THE MONEY.` · `A GUIDE WHO WAS WAITING.` · `THE DOG WENT WITH THEM.` · `RAPHAEL: GOD HEALS.` · then, large: `HEALING WALKING BESIDE THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a traveler in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is on a road right now, or about to be. Someone driving a long way, flying out, moving cities, starting a new job, or making a harder kind of journey, through an illness or a loss. Picture them on the road, and picture someone walking beside them whom they might not recognize. Catholics often ask Raphael to pray for travelers, the way they'd ask a friend. If you pray, you can ask Raphael to walk with this person today. If you don't, just hold them in mind, arriving safely. The bell holds the time.
Tobit's journey. The story of a blind father, his son Tobias sent on the road, a faithful dog, and a guide who was the angel Raphael, whose name means God heals. Today's word.
Your line: raphael walks with you. Today, send a message to someone on a journey, any kind, and tell them they're not walking alone. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

438.title: The wedding night prayer (Tobit 8)
438.hook: Tobias and Sara pray together before anything else
438.howItsDone: The prayer of Tobias and Sara (Tobit 8) is among the Old Testament readings couples may choose for a Catholic wedding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tobias set out with a dog and a guide who was really an angel. Your line was raphael walks with you. Who did you hold in mind on their journey? Day four hundred thirty-eight.

Remember Sara, the young woman in Media who prayed to die on the same day as Tobit? Here's why. She had been married seven times, and each husband died on the wedding night, before the marriage began, killed, the book says, by a demon named Asmodeus. Even her father's maid taunted her for it. On the road, Raphael tells Tobias: she's your kinswoman, and you should marry her. Then he brings him to her father Raguel's house. Tobias has heard the stories. He's afraid. Who wouldn't be? Husband number eight.
screen: `SEVEN HUSBANDS, SEVEN WEDDING NIGHTS.` → `RAPHAEL SAYS: MARRY HER.` → `HUSBAND NUMBER EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Raguel agrees, the contract is written, there's a meal. Then the young couple are shown to their room. Tobias does what Raphael told him: he puts part of the fish from the Tigris on the coals, and the smoke drives the demon away, and Raphael binds it far off in the desert of Egypt. And then, before anything else, Tobias turns to his bride and says, in effect: Sara, get up. Let's pray, the two of us, that the Lord will have mercy on us. And they pray together. The prayer remembers where marriage began: God made Adam, and gave him Eve as a helper, and said it isn't good for the man to be alone. Tobias says he's taking Sara not out of lust but in truth, with a sincere heart. And they ask God for mercy, and to grow old together. In the Latin text the Douay follows, they go further and spend three nights in prayer before they sleep together. The Greek text keeps the prayer short. Either way, the first thing these two did as a married couple was pray. Meanwhile, down the hall, poor Raguel has been up in the night, quietly digging a grave, just in case. In the morning he sends a maid to peek in, and she finds them both asleep and well. So he has the grave filled in before anyone sees it, blesses God, and throws a wedding feast. This prayer of Tobias and Sara is one of the readings couples can choose for a Catholic wedding.
screen: `THE SMOKE, AND THE DEMON BOUND.` · `SARA, GET UP. LET'S PRAY.` · `MERCY, AND TO GROW OLD TOGETHER.` · `A GRAVE DUG, THEN FILLED IN.` · then, large: `BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE, THEY PRAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray with someone you love, or hold them close in silence. Settle, and breathe. If someone you love is near you right now and willing, you could sit together and pray something you both know, an Our Father, or simply a moment of silence side by side. If you're alone, think of the person you'd most want beside you. A spouse, a parent, a child, a friend. Picture sitting down together before the day's business begins, the way Tobias and Sara did. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy on the two of you. The bell holds the time.
Tobias. The bridegroom who, before anything else on his wedding night, prayed with Sara for mercy and to grow old together. Today's word.
Your line: pray together first. Today, before a meal or a big conversation with someone you love, stop for one shared moment first. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

439.title: Judith (Judith 8–13)
439.hook: a widow rebukes the elders for testing God and saves her city
439.howItsDone: Catholics hear Judith in the Liturgy of the Hours and at Mass, and the Church's liturgy applies the praise given to Judith, blessed above all women, to the Virgin Mary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tobias and Sara began their marriage on their knees, and Raguel filled in the grave. Your line was pray together first. Who did you stop with, before the day began? Day four hundred thirty-nine.

A small hill town called Bethulia is under siege. A huge army under the general Holofernes has surrounded it and cut off the springs. The cisterns are running dry. Children are fainting in the streets. The people gather around the town's leaders and shout: surrender. Better to be slaves and alive than to watch our children die of thirst. So the chief elder, Ozias, makes a deal with them. Hold out five more days. If God hasn't helped us by then, we'll open the gates. It sounds reasonable. It sounds like faith, even. And a widow in the town hears about it.
screen: `A HILL TOWN UNDER SIEGE.` → `THE SPRINGS CUT OFF.` → `FIVE MORE DAYS, THEN SURRENDER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Judith, which simply means a Jewish woman, a woman of Judea. Her husband had died of sunstroke at the barley harvest, and for over three years she'd lived as a widow, fasting and praying, wealthy and widely respected; nobody, the book says, spoke an ill word of her. She sends for the elders, and she doesn't soften it. Who are you, she asks, to put God to the test? You've set a deadline for the mercy of the Lord, and appointed him a day of your own choosing. God isn't a man, to be threatened or bargained with. If he wants to save us, he can, in his own time. Then she tells them she has a plan, and that they're not to ask what it is. She prays, takes off her widow's clothes, dresses in her finest, and walks out of the town gate with her maid, straight into the enemy camp. She tells Holofernes she's come to help him win. He is charmed. On the fourth night he throws a banquet, drinks more than he ever has, and falls asleep, and Judith, alone in the tent, takes his own sword and kills him. She carries his head back to the town in her food bag, and the army, leaderless, breaks and runs. It's a hard, bloody story, and the book doesn't look away. It also doesn't read like a chronicle: it opens with Nabuchodonosor as king of the Assyrians, reigning in Nineveh, and some readers, Catholic scholars among them, take details like that as signs of a story told to teach. What it teaches is clear: when the leaders gave up, a widow didn't.
screen: `JUDITH: A WOMAN OF JUDEA.` · `YOU SET A DEADLINE FOR GOD'S MERCY.` · `INTO THE ENEMY CAMP.` · `A STORY TOLD TO TEACH.` · then, large: `WHEN THE LEADERS GAVE UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find where you might need to speak up. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place you belong where the people in charge have quietly given up. A team at work, a parish committee, a family, a school, a town. Maybe they've set a deadline for hope. Maybe they've decided nothing can change. Don't plan anything dramatic. Just ask what one respectful, honest sentence you could say to them would be, the way Judith called the elders and told them the truth. If you pray, you can ask for her courage. The bell holds the time.
Judith. The widow of Bethulia who rebuked the elders for putting God on a deadline, and then went out and saved her city. Today's word.
Your line: a widow saved the city. Today, say the honest sentence you found, kindly, to someone who has given up. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

440.title: In the hand of God (Wisdom 3:1–9)
440.hook: the souls of the just are in the hand of God, read at many funerals
440.howItsDone: Wisdom 3:1–9 is among the Old Testament readings a family may choose for a Catholic funeral, and it is also read on feasts of martyrs and on All Souls' Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judith told the elders they couldn't put God on a deadline, and walked out the gate. Your line was a widow saved the city. Did you say your honest sentence? Day four hundred forty.

"But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them." It's one of the readings a family may choose for a Catholic funeral, so if you've heard it, it may have been from a lectern, near a coffin, on a hard day. Some people hear it only there, without ever learning where it comes from. It comes from one of the seven books we met this week: the Book of Wisdom, a book that argues with people who think death ends everything.
screen: `READ FROM THE LECTERN.` → `ON A HARD DAY.` → `FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Wisdom speaks in the voice of a king who prayed for wisdom, the voice tradition gives to Solomon, though the book never names him. It has come down to us in Greek, and some readers place its writer among the Greek-speaking Jews of Alexandria. Chapter two gives the other side first. It lets the ungodly speak, and they sound very modern. Life is short and then nothing, they say. Let's enjoy ourselves, and if a just man gets in our way and makes us feel bad, let's crush him and see if his God saves him. Then chapter three answers. The souls of the just are in the hand of God. And the Douay goes on: "In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die: and their departure was taken for misery: And their going away from us, for utter destruction: but they are in peace." Seemed. To someone looking from outside, it's the end, a loss, a ruin. But they are in peace. The writer says their hope is full of immortality. God tested them like gold in a furnace, and received them like an offering. And at their visitation, the Douay says, the just shall shine, and run to and fro like sparks among the reeds. Here hope reaches past death in so many words, and you can see why the Church reaches for it at funerals, and on the feasts of martyrs. And the image is plain. A hand. Not a cloud, not a throne, not a distant place. A hand, the way you'd hold something small and precious so nothing can get at it.
screen: `A KING'S VOICE, IN GREEK.` · `THE UNGODLY SPEAK FIRST.` · `THEY SEEMED TO DIE.` · `GOLD IN THE FURNACE, SPARKS IN THE REEDS.` · then, large: `BUT THEY ARE IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who has died. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind. A grandparent, a friend, a parent, a child, someone whose funeral you remember, or someone whose funeral you missed. Say their name quietly. Picture their hands, if you can remember them. Then picture those hands held in a larger hand, safe, so that nothing can touch them now. If you pray, you can pray for them; Catholics have an old prayer for this that begins eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord. If you don't, just hold their name for a while. The bell holds the time.
Immortality. The hope Wisdom says is full and unshaken for the just who have died: they seemed to die, but they are in peace. Today's word.
Your line: they are in peace. Today, say the name of the person you remembered out loud to someone else, and tell one thing about them. Day four hundred forty.

441.title: Praying for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:43–46)
441.hook: Judas Maccabeus sends an offering for the fallen; Catholics see here the practice of praying for the dead
441.howItsDone: Catholics have Masses offered for the dead, pray for the souls in purgatory, and keep All Souls' Day, and 2 Maccabees 12:43–46 is among the readings for funerals and Masses for the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Book of Wisdom: the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and they are in peace. Your line was they are in peace. Whose name did you say out loud? Day four hundred forty-one, the end of the week, and the end of a block.

Judas Maccabeus has led a Jewish revolt against a Greek king who tried to stamp out their faith, and after one battle his men go out the next day to gather the bodies of their fallen friends and bring them home for burial. And under the coats of the slain they find small objects consecrated to the idols of a nearby city, things the law forbade. Amulets, maybe. Charms for luck in battle. Everyone suddenly understands why these men fell. It's a terrible moment. What do you do for the dead now?
screen: `GATHERING THE FALLEN.` → `CHARMS UNDER THEIR COATS.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO FOR THEM NOW?`

segments.voice: They don't condemn them and walk away. They turn to prayer, asking that the sin they had committed be forgotten. Then Judas takes up a collection among the soldiers and sends silver to Jerusalem, for a sacrifice to be offered for the sins of the dead. And the writer stops to explain why. If he hadn't hoped that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been pointless to pray for the dead. And then the line that gives us our carry, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." Wholesome is the Latin salubris: health-giving, good for you. The Catholic Church points to this passage when it teaches that those who die in God's friendship but still need purifying can be helped by the prayers of the living, the teaching called purgatory. That's why Catholics have Masses said for the dead, pray for the souls in purgatory, and keep a day, All Souls', for remembering them all. The Orthodox also pray for the dead. Protestant churches differ among themselves on prayer for the dead, and Protestant Bibles, if they print Maccabees at all, place it among the Apocrypha. And now, a look back. This week: the Benedicite, the books between, Raphael on the road, a wedding night prayer, Judith, the hand of God, and prayers for the dead. And this whole block of fifty days: Deborah, Gideon, Ruth, Hannah, Samuel, David, Solomon, Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Jonah, Job, the wisdom books and the seven. Tomorrow we turn to the Gospel of Luke.
screen: `THEY PRAYED FOR THE SIN TO BE FORGOTTEN.` · `SILVER SENT FOR A SACRIFICE.` · `SALUBRIS: HEALTH-GIVING.` · `FIFTY DAYS OF KINGS AND PROPHETS.` · then, large: `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your dead. Settle, and breathe. Let the people you've lost come to mind, one at a time. Don't rush. Grandparents. Parents. Friends. Someone who died young. Someone you had unfinished business with. Say each name quietly as it comes. Don't hold back the complicated ones; Judas didn't. If you pray, you can pray for each of them as Catholics do, asking God's mercy on each name. If you don't, let naming them be enough. The bell holds the time.
Judas Maccabeus. He sent an offering for his fallen soldiers after amulets were found on their bodies, and Catholics see here the practice of praying for the dead. Today's word.
Your line: a holy and wholesome thought. Today, write down the names you said, and keep the list somewhere you'll see it. Day four hundred forty-one.
